title: A Land Without the Troubles?
gist: Reviewing Jan Carson's novel 'Few and Far Between,' Maxine Davey uses the book's magical-realist premise (a partially drained Lough Neagh) to argue Northern Ireland's Troubles-era trauma was never formally processed via truth-and-reconciliation, leaving a culture of silence that both enabled the peace process and left deep, still-unresolved social wounds — reopened by Brexit and now compounded by a genuine environmental crisis (toxic algae) and rising anti-immigrant sentiment.

themes.theme: Unprocessed trauma as the structural legacy of the Troubles

insights.claim: No formal truth and reconciliation process followed Northern Ireland's Troubles, and without a real outlet to address trauma, the state left society-wide wounds to fester with an almost willful blindness — a culture of silence that functioned as a deliberate strategy to transition suspected former IRA members into legitimate political actors and enable negotiations with the British government, but also had deadly consequences.
insights.speaker: Maxine Davey
insights.so_what: Identifies the absence of formal reconciliation as a specific, durable structural risk factor for renewed instability in Northern Ireland — relevant precedent for post-conflict societies where peace was purchased via silence rather than accountability.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Yet despite the peace process'

insights.claim: As of 2017, nearly 4,000 people had died by suicide in Northern Ireland since the Good Friday Agreement — more than were killed during the entire duration of the Troubles.
insights.speaker: Maxine Davey
insights.so_what: A striking, verifiable statistic showing post-conflict suicide deaths have exceeded conflict-era violent deaths — a hard data point on the ongoing public-health and social cost of unresolved Troubles-era trauma, relevant to Northern Ireland public-health policy and funding debates.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'But while a buried gun's not killing anybody'

insights.claim: The 1998 Omagh bombing killed 29 people just four months after the Good Friday Agreement, the deadliest terrorist attack in Northern Ireland's history, and a Northern Ireland inquiry established in 2024 to determine whether British state authorities could have prevented it has dragged on for two years, impeded by the difficulty of collecting over a quarter-century-old evidence.
insights.speaker: Maxine Davey
insights.so_what: An active, unresolved state-accountability inquiry into a 1998 attack is a live legal/political risk still working through Northern Ireland's institutions nearly three decades later — a marker of how long-tailed post-conflict accountability processes can run.

insights.claim: The 2016 Brexit referendum resurfaced jurisdictional and cultural frictions that made Northern Ireland's peace 'wobblier with each passing year,' threatening the stability of the Irish border where no physical checkpoints have existed since the Good Friday Agreement; over 10 years after the referendum, British leaders still have not fully solved how to regulate cross-border trade without imposing checks reminiscent of the Troubles.
insights.speaker: Maxine Davey
insights.so_what: A decade-plus unresolved Irish border trade-regulation problem tied directly to Brexit is a persistent structural risk for UK-EU relations and Northern Ireland political stability — relevant for ongoing UK-EU trade negotiation risk.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'In Carson's timeline, just as in ours'

insights.claim: Political violence between Catholics and Protestants is rare in Northern Ireland today, but the country's lingering divisions remain visible in towering 'peace walls' still separating communities, street art staking claims to identity, and Palestinian and Israeli flags projecting local tensions onto global conflicts — with rising anti-immigrant sentiment today, especially among Protestant loyalists.
insights.speaker: Maxine Davey
insights.so_what: Documents a specific, current social-tension vector (anti-immigrant sentiment among Protestant loyalists) layering onto unresolved sectarian divisions — a factor relevant for assessing Northern Ireland's susceptibility to future unrest.
insights.quote: When they scratch the surface—which they frequently do, mostly with words but sometimes with fists—there is still a deep divide running through the heart of the place.
insights.locator: quote attributed to the character Marion

themes.theme: Historical policy failure as fictional premise

insights.claim: The novel's premise is grounded in a real 1958 proposal by Northern Irish leader Terence O'Neill to drain Lough Neagh, the largest lake in the British Isles, and build a new town where Protestants and Catholics could work alongside one another — a scheme quickly deemed unworkable in reality but imagined as partly realized in the novel.
insights.speaker: Maxine Davey
insights.so_what: A minor but real historical footnote (the 1958 Lough Neagh drainage proposal) illustrating the long history of ambitious, ultimately unworkable Northern Irish reconciliation schemes — useful historical color for understanding the region's institutional memory around integration attempts.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Few and Far Between imagines an alternate history'
